title: The Road to Emmaus
lead: Jesus can walk beside a person who has lost hope long before that person recognizes Him.
questions: Who among the people close to me is walking toward their own Emmaus right now, and what would it mean to catch up with them and walk alongside, instead of calling after them from a distance?
How does Jesus’ order of things look in my life: do I listen all the way to the end before I open the Scriptures, or do I start rushing sooner?
Whom should I invite to my table, since eyes that stayed closed during the lecture are opened at the table?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: It is still resurrection Sunday. The tomb is empty, the news has been announced, and yet two disciples leave Jerusalem and head for Emmaus, walking away from the community and from the cause they had poured years of their lives into. In their conversation comes a sentence that holds every disappointment of faith: “But we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel.” Hope in the past tense. And they know all the facts: the empty tomb, the women, the angels. Full information, zero hope; between the news and the heart lies a road that someone has to walk with a person.

And it is these two whom the risen Lord catches up with. He doesn’t reveal Himself in glory; He comes up like any traveler and asks, “What are you discussing so intently as you walk along?” He listens to all their bitterness, to the very end, though He knows how the story ends. He has an unanswerable argument up His sleeve: His own hands. Instead, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself”: the cross was not a catastrophe but a fulfillment. Their faith was to stand on the Word, not on a spectacle, because hope built on an experience melts away with the experience. Toward evening “He seemed to be going farther”: He doesn’t invite Himself in; He waits for “Stay with us.” And at the table the guest becomes the host: “He took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to them. Then their eyes were opened.” They recognized Him not during the lecture, but in the breaking of the bread, in a gesture they had seen a hundred times.

The diagnosis comes in hindsight: “Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” Hope came back before recognition did. And that very hour, at night, uphill, they walk the seven miles back to Jerusalem, because news like this can’t wait until breakfast. After meeting the risen Lord, you can tell a person by the direction they are walking.

This story is a manual for walking with people who have lost hope: catch up with those going the wrong way, walk beside them, ask, listen to the end, open the Scriptures, sit down at the table. In exactly that order. We like to start by correcting people, and then we wonder why they keep walking toward their own Emmaus.

It is still the same Sunday we looked at yesterday. The tomb is already empty, the women have already brought the news, Peter has already seen the linen cloths. And yet two disciples pack up and leave Jerusalem. They are going to Emmaus, a village about seven miles away, and every step takes them farther from the community, from the place where it all happened, and from the cause they had poured several years of their lives into. This is the direction of someone who has stopped waiting. The gospel of the resurrection has, right at its center, a story about two people who on resurrection day were walking in exactly the opposite direction. And it was these two whom the risen Lord caught up with.

sections.heading: But We Were Hoping
paragraphs: Luke lets us overhear their conversation, and in it is a sentence that holds every disappointment of faith: “But we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel.” We were hoping. Hope in the past tense. These two know everything we know: they can recite the facts about the empty tomb, about the women, about the angels who said He was alive, about the companions who went to check and “found it just as the women had described.” Full information, zero hope. This is one of the most important observations in the whole story: you can have all the correct data about the resurrection and still be walking to Emmaus. Facts don’t turn into hope automatically; between the news and the heart lies a road that someone has to walk with a person. Luke doesn’t smooth over their disappointment, either; he just quotes it. They had been hoping for Israel’s redeemer, for political liberation, and from where they stood, Friday had wiped all that out. The road they were walking was itself a lesson in caution: a generation earlier the area around Emmaus had run with blood after a messianic uprising was crushed. These two knew how hopes in deliverers tend to end.

sections.heading: He Came Up and Walked with Them
paragraphs: What Jesus does here is a masterpiece of gentleness. He doesn’t reveal Himself in glory; He doesn’t open with “It’s Me, everything is explained.” He comes up like an ordinary traveler and asks a question: “What are you discussing so intently as you walk along?” And then a second one: “What things?” The risen Lord of the world, who knows incomparably more about what happened in Jerusalem than they do, asks and listens. He lets them tell the whole story of their disappointment, mistakes and bitterness included, all the way to the end. We saw this style at the well in Samaria: the conversation starts with a question, not a lecture. You don’t help someone who has lost hope by cutting them off mid-sentence with the correct answer. You help by walking beside them and listening to the end, even when you already know how it ends. Luke adds that “their eyes were kept from recognizing Him.” They didn’t recognize Him, and there was a purpose in that: they were to hear Him first, and only then to see Him.

sections.heading: Was It Not Necessary
paragraphs: Only after they have poured everything out does Jesus begin to speak, and He does something that ought to astonish us. He has an unanswerable argument up His sleeve: His own hands, with the marks of the nails. All He had to do was show them. Instead, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself.” The risen Lord leads a Bible study. A walking, hours-long study of the Old Testament, in which the Author of the events Himself shows that the cross was not a catastrophe but a fulfillment: “Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?” That choice of method was no accident. The faith of these two was to stand on the Scriptures, not on a spectacle; Jesus Himself once said in a parable that those who will not listen to Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead. On the road to Emmaus He proved that sentence from the other side: first He opened the Scriptures to them, and only then their eyes. The order is a signpost for all time: hope built on an experience melts away with the experience; hope built on the Word has something to stand on when experiences fail.

sections.heading: Stay with Us
paragraphs: Toward evening they reach Emmaus, and Luke records a small, deeply respectful detail: Jesus “seemed to be going farther.” He doesn’t invite Himself in. The same God who caught up with them on the road will not cross the threshold of their home without an invitation. Luke says the disciples “pleaded with Him”: they kept the stranger for the night, as the good tradition of hospitality required. And there is a hidden lesson in that: their first healthy impulse in three days was a move toward another person. Hope began to return to them at exactly the moment they stopped being absorbed in nothing but their own heartbreak and invited someone to their table. Only at their “Stay with us, for it is nearly evening” does Jesus go in. And at the table the roles suddenly reverse: the guest acts like the host. “He took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to them.” Four verbs we heard three days ago over five loaves on the grass, and which the church has heard ever since at every Lord’s Supper. “Then their eyes were opened and they recognized Jesus.” Not during the lecture, though the lecture was necessary; in the breaking of the bread. They recognized Him in a gesture they had seen a hundred times: the everyday act of passing food around. And in that same moment “He disappeared from their sight,” because the sign had done its work: from now on they were not to see but to believe, and to feed on that recognition at every shared table.

sections.heading: Were Not Our Hearts Burning
paragraphs: The two disciples react at once, and beautifully. First comes a diagnosis in hindsight: “Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” Something was already on fire in them on the road, before they understood why; hope was returning before recognition did. Then comes action: “they got up that very hour and returned to Jerusalem.” That very hour, meaning at night, and uphill: the road from Emmaus to Jerusalem is a long climb stretching for miles. That morning they had walked down it slowly, weighed down by a lost cause. Now they climb it at night, without lanterns, some seven miles, because news like this can’t wait until breakfast. You can tell someone who has met the risen Lord by the direction they are walking. In Jerusalem they find the community already ablaze with the same news: “The Lord has indeed risen and has appeared to Simon!” Their private discovery turns out to be part of something bigger; separate stories of encounter come together into the single confession of the church. Incidentally, that line about Simon is one of the strongest arguments for the reliability of these accounts: the risen Lord’s meeting with the leading apostle is dispatched in half a sentence, with no scene at all. People who invent legends expand exactly these moments; people who record eyewitness accounts write down as much as they were told. And one last detail: Luke remembered the name of one of the two travelers, Cleopas. The plot doesn’t need that name. The simplest explanation is that Luke is citing his source. This story was told to him by a man who walked it, step by step, on his own two feet.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: This story is a manual for walking with people who have lost hope, and it is worth reading as a program. First, Jesus caught up with those going the wrong way; He didn’t wait for them to come back or call after them from behind the walls of Jerusalem. Then He asked and listened to the end, though He knew the answers better than they did. Then He opened the Scriptures: He didn’t moralize; He showed the meaning in what had looked like a catastrophe. And finally He let Himself be invited to the table, and there He let Himself be recognized. The road, listening, the Word, the table: in exactly that order. We like to start with the third step, or jump straight to correcting people, and then we wonder why they keep walking toward their own Emmaus. If someone close to you, maybe someone from your church, is right now walking in the direction away from the community, this story tells you what to do: catch up, walk alongside, ask, listen to the end. And don’t skip the table, because at the table eyes are opened that stayed closed during the lecture. And if you are the one on the road to Emmaus today, remember one thing from this story: the risen Lord walks that road too. Even if your sentence “I was hoping” is stuck in the past tense, Someone has already come up beside you and is walking with you, and your heart may be burning before you understand why.
